turns.prompt_text: I own a google chromebook 11, I would like to install linux on it
turns.response_html:
You have a few options for installing Linux on a Chromebook, but the "best" method depends heavily on exactly which "Chromebook 11" you have (HP, Dell, and Acer all made models with this name) and how old it is.

The three main methods are listed below, starting with the easiest and safest.

Method 1: The Official Way (Crostini)

Best for: Chromebooks made after 2019. Most modern Chromebooks have a built-in feature called "Linux (Beta)" or "Linux Development Environment." This runs Linux in a safe container without requiring you to "hack" your device.

  1. Open your Chromebook Settings.
  2. On the left sidebar, click Advanced -> Developers.
  3. If you see an option for Linux development environment, click Turn On.
  4. Follow the on-screen prompts. Once finished, a "Terminal" app will appear in your app drawer. You can use this to install Linux apps (e.g., sudo apt install gimp).

If you do not see this option, your device is likely too old for the official method. You should try Method 2.

Method 2: The Enthusiast Way (Crouton)

Best for: Older Chromebooks (2013–2018) or ARM-based devices. Crouton allows you to run a full Linux desktop (like Ubuntu or XFCE) side-by-side with ChromeOS. You can switch between them instantly with a keyboard shortcut.

Warning: This requires "Developer Mode," which is less secure and will wipe your local data (Downloads folder) upon setup.

  1. Back up your data.
  2. Enter Developer Mode:
    • Hold Esc + Refresh (circular arrow key) + tap Power.
    • When the "Chrome OS is missing or damaged" screen appears, press Ctrl + D, then Enter.
    • Your Chromebook will wipe itself and reboot (this takes about 15 minutes).
  3. Install Crouton:
    • Download the crouton script (click the link on the GitHub page).
    • Open the ChromeOS terminal (press Ctrl + Alt + T, type shell, and hit Enter).
    • Run the installer command (example for XFCE desktop): sudo install -Dt /usr/local/bin -m 755 ~/Downloads/crouton && sudo crouton -t xfce
  4. Once installed, start Linux by typing sudo startxfce4 in the shell.

Method 3: Full Replacement (MrChromebox)

Best for: Advanced users who want to delete ChromeOS entirely. If you want your Chromebook to behave like a standard laptop (booting directly into Linux Mint, Manjaro, etc.), you must modify the device's firmware.

  1. This often requires removing a "Write Protect Screw" from the motherboard inside the case.
  2. You will need to run the MrChromebox Firmware Utility Script to install a custom BIOS (UEFI).
  3. You then install Linux from a USB drive just like a normal PC. Note: This is risky. If something goes wrong, you could "brick" the laptop.

Recommendation

Check Method 1 first. If "Linux development environment" is missing from your settings, your "Chromebook 11" is likely an older model (like the HP Chromebook 11 G1-G5 or Dell Chromebook 11 3120). In that case, Method 2 (Crouton) is the most reliable way to get a functional Linux desktop without opening up the case.

Crucial First Step Because "Chromebook 11" is a generic name used by HP, Dell, and Acer, you need to know your specific Board Name (e.g., "Kip", "Setzer", "Wolf") to know which Linux versions are compatible.

... How to Find the Model Name / Number of a Chromebook Computer ...

This video is relevant because it shows you how to find your specific model name/board ID, which is required to determine if your specific "Chromebook 11" supports the easy Linux installation method (Crostini) or requires the more complex ones.
